name: Baghdad
info: Baghdad is the capital of Iraq, on the Tigris. Founded by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur in 762, it became a centre of learning and trade, was sacked by the Mongols in 1258 and became the capital of Iraq in 1921.

facts.founded: 30 July 762, commissioned by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur, on a site settled since at least the Neo-Babylonian period
facts.where: On both banks of the Tigris on a flat alluvial plain in central Iraq
facts.known: The Round City of al-Mansur; the Abbasid capital; the House of Wisdom and the translation movement; its libraries and madrasas; the Mongol sack of 1258; the Arabian Nights; a large Jewish community until the mid 20th century; the capital of modern Iraq
facts.today: Baghdad is the capital and largest city of Iraq.

t: Al-Mansur commissioned Baghdad on 30 July 762 as the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate, on a site that had been settled since at least the Neo-Babylonian period.
For two centuries it was one of the largest cities in the world and a centre of translation, science, law and trade, until political divisions and the loss of provinces slowed its growth.
The Mongols under Hulegu sacked it in 1258 and ended the Abbasid Caliphate, and later Timur, the Safavids and the Ottomans held it before it became the capital of Iraq in 1921.
dyk: Bricks stamped with the name and titles of Nebuchadnezzar II have been found along the west bank of the Tigris at Baghdad, so the site was in use more than a thousand years before al-Mansur built his Round City.
ev: Al-Mansur commissions the Round City on 30 July
The House of Wisdom and the translation movement flourish under al-Ma'mun
The Seljuk leader Tughril Beg takes Baghdad from the Buyids
The Mongols under Hulegu capture Baghdad on 10 February and end the Abbasid Caliphate
The Ottomans take Baghdad and make it the administrative capital of Ottoman Iraq
British forces capture Baghdad on 11 March
Baghdad becomes the capital of the independent Kingdom of Iraq

sections.origins:
Baghdad lies on the Tigris in central Iraq, on a flat plain of alluvial origin. The site was occupied before the Abbasids built there. An extensive facing of Neo-Babylonian brickwork has been identified along the west bank of the river, with bricks stamped with the name and titles of Nebuchadnezzar II, and Assyrian geographical lists record a place with a name very similar to Baghdad, which probably refers to a town on the same ground. A boundary stone from the reign of Merodach-baladan I, in the 12th century BCE, gives the name as Bag-da-du. The origin of the name is disputed. Arab authors looked for it in Middle Persian, and the commonest meaning they gave was "bestowed by God"; modern scholars generally favour this reading, a compound of bagh, "god", and dād, "given".

The Abbasids, after their victory over the Umayyads, wanted a capital of their own. On 30 July 762 the caliph al-Mansur commissioned a new city north of Ctesiphon, the Sasanian capital, with the guidance of the Iranian Barmakids. The site controlled routes along the Tigris and had abundant water. According to al-Tabari, Christian monks had foretold that a lord named Miklas would build a great city there, and al-Mansur had been called Miklas as a child. The astrologers Naubakht, a Zoroastrian, and Mashallah, a Jew from Khorasan, are said to have chosen the day under the sign of Leo. Al-Mansur named his city Madinat as-Salam, the "City of peace"; by the 11th century Baghdad was almost the only name used.
sections.growth:
Within a generation of its founding Baghdad had become a centre of learning and commerce. Its position on the Khurasan road and the Tigris linked it to trade routes towards China, India and Armenia, and its water supply was plentiful. The city grew so large that it was divided into three judicial districts: the Round City, al-Karkh (al-Sharqiyya) and Askar al-Mahdi. Al-Mansur moved the markets to al-Karkh, away from the Round City, and officials called muhtasib checked weights, measures and the quality of goods. A banking system developed, the city's suitability for paper production lowered the cost of books, and libraries and bookshops appeared.

Baghdad is likely to have been the largest city in the world from shortly after its foundation until the 930s, when it tied with Córdoba. Estimates of its size vary widely. Several put the population at over a million at its peak, and some at between 1.2 million and 2 million by the 10th century, while others give between 300,000 and 500,000 for the 10th century. Growth slowed as the caliphs moved the capital to Samarra, provinces were lost and other powers dominated the city. After the Mongol sack Baghdad was rebuilt and flourished under the Ilkhanate, but never rose to its former standing. In the later 18th century, under Mamluk government, it revived somewhat, and in the 1970s a sharp rise in the price of petroleum brought a new period of prosperity, with new sewers, water supplies and highways. Its population grew from an estimated 145,000 in 1900 to 580,000 in 1950.
sections.rulers:
Baghdad was the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate from 762. The caliphs moved to Samarra for a time, from 836 to 892, and from the 10th century the city was dominated by outside powers: the Iranian Buyids (945 to 1055) and then the Seljuk Turks (1055 to 1135). Tughril Beg took the city in 1055 and the Seljuks ruled as sultans in the name of the Abbasid caliphs, whose protector he considered himself. In 1058 the general al-Basasiri, an adherent of the Ismailis, held it for the Fatimid caliph. After the Mongol conquest of 1258 it was ruled by the Ilkhanate, then taken by Timur in 1393 and 1401. It then became a provincial capital under the Jalayirids (1400 to 1411), the Qara Qoyunlu (1411 to 1469), the Aq Qoyunlu (1469 to 1508) and the Safavids, who held it from 1508 or 1509 until the Ottomans took it in 1534.

The Safavids retook it in 1624 and Murad IV recaptured it for the Ottomans in 1638. In the later 18th century the city was under Mamluk government, and direct Ottoman rule was reimposed in 1831 under Ali Riza Pasha. The municipality was established in 1868, and in 1869 Midhat Pasha began the reforms of the Tanzimat. Baghdad was the headquarters of the Sixth Corps of the Ottoman army. British forces captured it on 11 March 1917, and in 1921, under the Mandate, it became the capital of a British-protected monarchy; Iraq became independent in 1932. The monarchy ended on 14 July 1958, when army units under Abdul-Karim Qasim seized the city and Iraq became a republic.
sections.life:
The Round City had four gates, named Kufa, Basra, Khurasan and Syria after the places they led to. Straight roads ran from the gates to the centre, lined with vaulted arcades of shops, and the heart of the city was kept as a royal preserve. The caliph's Golden Gate Palace stood at the centre under a green dome 48 metres high. Baghdad had night watchmen, lamplighters, health and market inspectors and a police force, and by the time of Harun al-Rashid a few thousand public baths. At night there were taverns, halls for chess and backgammon, plays, concerts and storytellers, whose tales were later told in the Arabian Nights.

Arabic was the language of science, but the scholars were also Persians, Syriacs, Nestorians, Jews and Arab Christians. The House of Wisdom, a centre for translating works into Arabic, had the largest collection of books in the world by the middle of the 9th century. Scholars in the city included the translator Hunayn ibn Ishaq, the mathematician al-Khwarizmi and the philosopher al-Kindi, and al-Jahiz contributed to Mu'tazili theology and al-Tabari to the interpretation of the Qur'an. The Hanafi and Hanbali schools of law drew scholars, and according to Ibn Battuta the residents were mostly Hanbalis. In the 19th century Baghdad was a leading centre of Jewish learning; the Jewish population reached 30,000 by 1884 and about 50,000 by 1900, over a quarter of the city's population.
sections.crises:
Baghdad was besieged in 812 to 813 in the civil war between the caliph al-Amin and his brother, and al-Amin was killed. It was besieged again in 865. On 10 February 1258 the Mongols led by Hulegu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, captured the city. Many quarters were ruined by fire, siege or looting, the Mongols killed most of the inhabitants, including the caliph al-Musta'sim, and the canals and dykes of the irrigation system were destroyed. The sack ended the Abbasid Caliphate. Timur occupied the city in 1393 and sacked it in 1401, when he is said to have spared almost no one and ordered each soldier to bring two severed heads. When the Safavid army entered in 1624 a massacre occurred. Plague and cholera struck repeatedly, and at times, it is said, two thirds of the population died.

On 1 and 2 June 1941, after the fall of Rashid Ali al-Gaylani's government, Jewish residents were attacked in the Farhud. Scholarly accounts commonly give about 180 Jews killed; the Iraqi commission reported 128 killed and 210 injured. In the Iran–Iraq War of the 1980s Iran fired missiles at Baghdad and power plants and refineries were damaged. In the Gulf War of 1991 coalition bombing damaged infrastructure, and a raid on 13 February killed at least 408 civilians at Amiriya. US forces took the city on 9 April 2003 after heavy bombing, and looting followed. An insurgency and a civil war between Sunni and Shia armed groups followed, and a further war lasted from 2013 to 2017.
sections.legacy:
The Round City left no visible remains: its walls were gone by 912, and there is no agreement on where it stood. What survives of medieval Baghdad is mostly in the Rusafa quarter. The Mustansiriyya Madrasa, founded in 1227 by the caliph al-Mustansir, stands in the Qushla area on the Tigris with Ottoman mosques, and the Baghdad Citadel, built in the 1430s under the Qara Qoyunlu, survived until the 20th century. The tombs of the imams Musa al-Kadhim and Muhammad at-Taqi at Kadhimiyya and the mosque of Abu Hanifa at Adhamiyya remain religious sites. Mutanabbi Street, named after the 10th century poet, is the historic centre of bookselling. The National Museum of Iraq, built under King Faisal, lost much of its collection to looting during the 2003 invasion.

Baghdad's reputation as a centre of learning rests on the House of Wisdom, the translation movement and the scholars of the 9th and 10th centuries, and many tales of the Arabian Nights are set in the city of that age. It was designated a UNESCO City of Literature in December 2015. Today Baghdad is the capital and largest city of Iraq, divided by the Tigris into Rusafa on the east bank and Karkh on the west.

summary: Baghdad was founded in 762 by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur and became a leading city of learning and trade. The Mongols sacked it in 1258, Timur in 1401, and it later passed to the Safavids and the Ottomans before becoming the capital of Iraq in the 20th century.
references: Guy Le Strange, Baghdad during the Abbasid Caliphate (Clarendon Press, 1900)
Gaston Wiet, Baghdad: metropolis of the Abbasid caliphate (University of Oklahoma Press, 1971)
Reuben Levy, A Baghdad Chronicle (Cambridge University Press, 2011)
notes: Population: the history article says over 1.5 million at the peak and 1.2 to 2 million in the 10th century; the city article says over a million at the peak; the history article's own later section says 300,000 to 500,000 by the 10th century. All left hedged as 'widely different'; no single figure given.
Foundation: history article gives 'four years (764 to 768)' and also 'by 766 complete'; I used neither completion date.

The Round City's fate: history article says it was partly ruined in the siege of 812 to 813 and its walls were gone by 912; the city article says it ceased to exist through the Mongol siege. I gave only the 912 point, attributed, and said there is no agreement on its site.
Samarra: the history article gives 808 to 819 and 836 to 892; I used only 836 to 892 because 808 to 819 looks doubtful (the city article repeats it); please check.

Safavid and Ottoman dates differ: Safavids 1508 (history) or 1509 (city article); Ottomans 1534 (both) or 1535 (city article, once); Safavid retaking 1623 or 1624; Murad IV 1638 or 1639. I used 1508 or 1509, 1534, 1624, 1638.
British capture: 11 March 1917 (history article) against 'until 1918' (city article). Used 1917.
Timur: 1393 and 1401 in both; the history article also lists a capture in 1394 and the city article a capture in 1394 in its list; omitted.
The dyk 'more than a thousand years' is my arithmetic from the 6th century BCE bricks to 762 CE; check.

Left out: Frank Lloyd Wright plan, OPEC, 1920 revolt, Ba'ath period details, 1990s uprisings, present-day population figures (8 million and 7 million disagree), the 2003 to 2020 terrorism figures, tourism and economy sections. Modern wars kept brief with no verdict.
The Safavid 'massacre' in 1624 is from the city article only, with no figure.
